term-system-call.d: A controlled transition through which user-mode code asks the kernel to perform an operation. A Win32 API may do substantial user-mode work before eventually reaching a system call.

term-soc.d: A single chip that holds most of a computer: CPU cores, a GPU, memory controllers, and often a security processor. Consoles and phones are built around one.

term-system-service-number.d: The number an ntdll.dll stub places in eax before syscall to choose which kernel routine runs. The numbers are internal to Windows and change between builds.

term-table-storage.d: A way of storing components in which entities with the same set of components share a table and each component has one column. A system reads a column straight through, but adding a component to one entity moves its whole row to another table. Compare sparse-set storage.

term-tap-controller.d: The 16-state machine inside every JTAG chip. At each rising edge of TCK the level of TMS picks one of two next states, and five clocks with TMS at 1 reach Test-Logic-Reset from any state.

term-tcp.d: A reliable, ordered byte-stream transport. It retransmits lost data but does not preserve application-message boundaries.

term-telemetry.d: Structured observations recorded over time, such as frame duration, state transitions, calls, or counters. Useful telemetry names units, clock, build, and capture boundaries.

term-temporal-coherence.d: The tendency for nearby moments to have related state. It can help tracking and validation, but it is not a guarantee: loading screens, respawns, and scene changes can invalidate yesterday’s assumptions instantly.

term-texture.d: An indexed image or general data resource sampled by GPU programs. A texture’s bytes need a format, dimensions, channel order, and sampling rules to have meaning.

term-thread.d: One line of execution running inside a process. A process can have several, all sharing the same memory but each keeping its own place in the code. Formally: an independently scheduled path of execution with its own registers, instruction pointer, and stack, sharing the rest of the process's resources.

term-thread-context.d: The register state needed to describe or resume a thread at a moment. Capturing or changing it safely normally requires controlled thread state.

term-thread-pool.d: A fixed set of threads that wait for small jobs in a queue and run them as they arrive, so slow work leaves the main thread alone. A common size is one fewer than the number of cores.

term-tick.d: One fixed step of a game's simulation. Every tick advances the world by the same slice of time, so behavior counted in ticks does not depend on the frame rate.

term-tilemap.d: A grid of tile numbers drawn as one rectangle per tile, taken from a sprite sheet, usually in a single draw call.

term-time-scale.d: A multiplier on game time: 1 is normal, 0.5 is slow motion, 2 is fast forward, and 0 is a pause. Every timer that counts game time stretches with it.

term-timing-check.d: A comparison of elapsed time against an expectation. Debugging, scheduling, power management, virtualization, and ordinary load all affect timing, so timing alone is a noisy signal.

term-toctou.d: A race in which state changes after it is checked but before the guarded operation uses it. The repair connects identity and freshness at the consuming boundary.

term-tls.d: Usually Transport Layer Security in networking: encryption and peer authentication layered over a transport. In PE and loader discussions, TLS can instead mean thread-local storage; context is essential.

term-tone-mapping.d: Compressing high-dynamic-range colors, which can exceed 1.0, into the 0 to 1 range a display can show. A simple rule, c ÷ (1 + c), squeezes bright values more than dim ones.

term-trampoline.d: A small executable bridge that copies displaced instructions and jumps back after a detour site. PC-relative operands may need relocation when copied to the trampoline.

term-transform.d: An operation that changes representation, position, orientation, or scale. Graphics transforms move coordinates between spaces; byte transforms may encode, compress, encrypt, or obfuscate data.

term-tlb.d: A small processor cache of recent address translations, so repeated accesses to the same pages skip the page-table walk.

term-trap-and-emulate.d: Running a guest kernel without privilege and letting the hypervisor catch and imitate each sensitive instruction. It needs every sensitive instruction to fault, which older x86 processors did not guarantee.

term-trust-boundary.d: A point where data or control crosses between components with different authority or assumptions. Validate at the boundary rather than relying on the sender to have done so.

term-turing-complete.d: Able to compute anything a Turing machine can in an idealized setting with enough time and memory. General-purpose languages such as Rust and Lua have that expressive power, although real runs have finite resources. A mod that ships a script is shipping a program whose effects also depend on what its host exposes.

term-turing-machine.d: An idealized model of computing: an unbounded tape of symbols, a head that reads and writes one cell, a current state, and a rule table saying what to write, where to move, and which state comes next. Real computers have finite memory, so they can carry out only the computations that fit their resources.

term-twos-complement.d: The usual way to store signed whole numbers: the leftmost bit's place value is negative (−128 in a byte), and every other bit keeps its normal value. So 0xFF is −1 as an i8 and 255 as a u8, and the CPU adds both with the same circuit.

term-type.d: How many bytes a value occupies, what its bits mean, and which operations are allowed on it. Raw bytes do not reveal their type; the instructions that read and use them do.

term-type-1-hypervisor.d: A hypervisor that runs directly on the hardware, with every operating system above it, such as Hyper-V, Xen, or VMware ESXi.

term-type-2-hypervisor.d: A hypervisor that runs as an application on a host operating system and relies on it for devices and scheduling, such as VirtualBox or VMware Workstation.

term-udp.d: A message-oriented transport with no built-in delivery, ordering, or duplicate suppression. Applications choose how to handle loss and reordering.

term-undecidable.d: Describes a question about programs that no single method answers correctly for every possible program, such as whether a program halts. Specific programs can often still be analyzed; the limit is on one method that works for all of them.

term-unicode.d: A standard assigning code points to text characters and symbols. UTF-8 and UTF-16 are encodings of those code points, not two different character sets.

term-unified-memory.d: One pool of memory shared by the CPU and the GPU, so both use the same bytes without copying data between separate memories. Consoles use it; most gaming PCs give the GPU its own video RAM.

term-unit-vector.d: A vector of length 1, used to store a direction. Dividing a vector by its own length produces one.

term-universal-turing-machine.d: A Turing machine that reads another machine's rule table from its tape and carries it out. It is the idea behind stored programs, interpreters, virtual machines, and emulators: change the data, not the machine.

term-unsafe.d: A small region where code accepts responsibility for facts the compiler cannot prove, such as raw-pointer validity or a foreign ABI. The boundary should state and check its preconditions, then expose a safer interface.

term-upvalue.d: Lua’s representation of a local variable captured by a closure. It lets the value outlive the stack frame that originally created it.

term-user-command.d: A sequenced sample of a player’s requested input, such as buttons, viewing direction, and movement intent. The server processes it under game rules; it is not a trusted claim about the final world state.

term-user-mode.d: The restricted CPU protection level where ordinary games and tools run. User-mode code accesses protected system resources through operating-system interfaces instead of directly controlling the kernel.

term-utility-ai.d: A way of choosing an action by giving every option a score computed from the current situation and running the highest-scoring one.

term-uv-coordinates.d: Two numbers from 0 to 1, called u and v, that name a point on a texture whatever its size in pixels. Direct3D, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU, and glTF put v = 0 at the top row, and classic OpenGL puts it at the bottom, so a texture can arrive upside down.

term-va.d: An address interpreted through one process’s current virtual-memory mappings. A live module VA is often its base plus an RVA.

term-vector.d: In math, an ordered set of components representing a direction, displacement, or point under a convention. In programming, “vector” can instead mean a growable contiguous sequence.

term-vector-table.d: A target-specific table of startup values and handler addresses. On the Cortex-M system in the firmware lesson, its first entry gives the initial stack pointer and its second the reset-handler address; it is not the first sequence of application instructions.

term-vertex.d: One input point of a graphics primitive together with attributes such as position, normal, color, and texture coordinates.

term-vsync.d: Making the present step wait for the display's next refresh. The frame rate is capped at the refresh rate and the picture does not tear.

term-view-cone.d: The range of directions an NPC can see: every direction within a set angle of its facing. Code usually tests it by comparing a dot product with the cosine of that angle.

term-view-matrix.d: The transform that expresses world coordinates relative to the camera. It is effectively the inverse of the camera’s world transform under the chosen convention.

term-viewport.d: The rectangle of a render target that a camera draws into. A split screen has one for each player, and projection has to use the viewport’s own size and origin, not the window’s.

term-virtual-machine.d: A software execution engine with its own instruction set and runtime state. Lua’s VM executes Lua bytecode; a hardware virtual machine instead emulates or partitions an entire computer. A system virtual machine, run by a hypervisor, instead presents a whole computer with the host’s own instruction set, so a guest operating system can run on it unmodified.

term-virtual-memory.d: The address abstraction that gives each process its own map of pages. The operating system can map pages to files, RAM, shared regions, or no backing at all.

term-virtual-key-code.d: The number Windows gives a key in window messages and key-state functions, produced from the scan code by the active keyboard layout. VK_A is 0x41.

term-vbs.d: The Windows feature that runs Windows above its own hypervisor in two virtual trust levels, so a secure world in VTL1 can protect memory and secrets from the normal kernel in VTL0.

term-vm-escape.d: A hypervisor bug that lets code in a guest run on the host, outside the guest's isolation and beyond any snapshot's reach.

term-vm-exit.d: The processor stopping a guest, saving its state, and running the hypervisor's handler with a reason code, for example after cpuid or an access to a guest physical page with no second-stage mapping.

term-vm-snapshot.d: A saved state of a whole virtual machine: its disk, frozen with later writes going to a delta file, and for a running machine its memory, processor registers, and device state.

term-vpk.d: An asset archive format used by Source games. Its directory identifies files and the location of their stored data, which may be in the directory archive or companion archives. A VPK does not define the server’s movement rules.

term-vptr.d: A compiler-generated pointer stored in many polymorphic C++ objects that points to a vtable. The exact placement and even existence are ABI and compiler details, not a language-level guarantee.

term-vtable.d: A compiler-generated table of virtual-function pointers and sometimes related metadata. One plausible table is evidence for a dynamic type, not complete proof of the original class hierarchy.

term-vulnerable-driver-blocklist.d: Microsoft's list of signed drivers with known exploitable bugs, which Windows refuses to load. It is on by default since the Windows 11 2022 update and enforced whenever memory integrity is on.

term-watchdog.d: A hardware timer that can reset a stalled device unless software services it as required. Its timeout and recovery policy must fit the device; logging or debugger pauses can affect its behaviour.

term-watchpoint.d: A debugger stop condition triggered when an address is read, written, or executed. Hardware supports only a small number and has size/alignment limits.

term-weighted-average.d: An average in which observations contribute different amounts. Repeated weighting can preserve older history without a fixed window boundary.

term-wildcard.d: A pattern position allowed to match any byte. Wildcards exclude unstable operands from a signature, but too many make the pattern ambiguous.

term-win32.d: The long-standing Windows application API family used by both 32-bit and 64-bit desktop programs. The name no longer means “32-bit applications only.”

term-window-message.d: A structured notification delivered to a Windows window procedure, such as input, paint, sizing, or lifecycle events. Posted messages are queued; sent messages may invoke the receiver synchronously.

term-window-procedure.d: The function a Windows program registers for a window, which the message loop calls with each message — a key press, a resize, a close request. It must return quickly, or the window stops responding.

term-world-space.d: The shared coordinate system in which scene objects are placed. An object’s model transform converts its local coordinates into world coordinates.

term-world-transform.d: An object’s position, turn, and scale in the world, derived once per frame by combining its local transform with its parents’. Writing to it changes nothing that lasts, because the next rebuild overwrites it from the local transform.

term-world-to-screen.d: The full conversion from a 3D world point through view and projection transforms, clipping, perspective division, and viewport mapping to a 2D screen location.

term-wrapping-arithmetic.d: Fixed-width arithmetic reduced modulo 2^N. Overflow wraps through the bit range, so recovering a transform must preserve the original width and operation order.

term-x86.d: The variable-length instruction-set family descended from Intel’s 8086. In this book, “x86” often means 32-bit mode, while x86-64 names the 64-bit extension.

term-x86-64.d: The 64-bit x86 architecture, also called AMD64. It expands registers, uses eight-byte pointers, and has different calling conventions and address rules from 32-bit x86.

term-xor.d: A bit operation that produces 1 when its two input bits differ. Applying the same XOR mask twice restores the original value; that reversibility alone does not make it secure encryption.

term-zero-terminated-string.d: A string whose end is marked by a zero code unit rather than a stored length. Readers need a maximum bound in case the terminator is missing.
